newsitem.title: JAPAN: Baseball fans swamp Tokyo Dome, lifting profits.
newsitem.headline: Baseball fans swamp Tokyo Dome, lifting profits.

text.p: A stunning comeback drive by the popular Yomiuri Giants baseball team into the Japan Series in October is likely to have helped break a seven-year streak of dwindling profits by the operators of its home stadium.
The fans poured into the Tokyo Dome in the second half of the season as the Giants roared back from 11-1/2 games out of first place to take the Central League title and reach the Japan Series.

"We expected to pull deeper into the black this year even without the Japan Series," said Shinji Kushiro, Tokyo Dome Corp executive director. "The games are definitely going to help make the profits concrete."

The first two games of the Japan Series were held in the 56,000-capacity Dome, also known as the Big Egg, in mid-October, followed by three more at the Pacific League champions Orix BlueWaves' home park in Kobe, western Japan.
The Giants lost the series four games to one.
The firm initially forecast a parent current profit of 5.1 billion yen ($44.7 million) for the year to January 31 against 4.85 billion yen ($42.5 million) the previous business year.
Current profit is pre-tax profit which includes gains and losses made on securities investments and other non-operating activities.

The 140 million yen ($1.22 million) worth of tickets, beer, food and Giants paraphernalia sold at each Japan Series game held at Japan's first domed stadium, translated into about 80 million yen ($701,000) in parent current profit, Kushiro said.
"Thanks to the two games, our profits may be augmented to about 5.3 billion yen ($46.4 million)," he said.

In addition to the windfall profits from the Japan Series, a new ride at the amusement park adjacent to the dome as well as four concerts by U.S pop superstar Michael Jackson scheduled for January were seen contributing to profits.

On a half-year basis, sales from the park, which installed Japan's first roller-coaster in 1955, jumped nearly 25 percent due to the new ride, the Tower Hacker, officials said. The ride is a hair-raising trip where shrieking passengers, strapped to chairs, plummet vertically from a height of 80 meters.

"The ride was built this spring and we thought the attention would last until summer at the latest, but the flow of visitors is showing no signs of abating," said Hisaaki Nakamura, manager of Tokyo Dome public relations department.
Analysts said Michael Jackson's HIStory World Tour '96 concerts were a plus, but only slightly so.

"The promoters are in charge of selling the tickets and Michael Jackson T-shirts and the Dome only gets paid rent and profits from sales of drinks and snacks," Yamaichi Securities analyst Hidekazu Umemura said.
Dome watchers said it was too early to say whether the upswing in parent current profits would continue.
"It's likely to be a one-time thing -- the Japan Series, a new ride, a major concert are all stimulants which will wear off after a while," Umemura said.
Dome officials said they are aware of the need to revamp their business and may opt to close some of their underperforming facilities, such as a swimming pool.

They also said they were finally going to start construction of a 1,000-room hotel on adjoining land which has been in the blueprint stage since the amusement park was first built in the middle of this century.
The company is waiting for government approval to start building the hotel, which it hopes will begin operations in 2000. ($1=114 yen)
